props.title: Eaten Alive
props.initialSlug: Crazed hotel owner feeds victims to his pet crocodile

sections.content: Eaten Alive (1976) represents Tobe Hooper's immediate follow-up to his groundbreaking The Texas Chain Saw Massacre (1974), delivering another sweat-soaked Southern Gothic nightmare. Set at the decrepit Starlight Hotel, the film follows deranged proprietor Judd (Neville Brand) who feeds unsuspecting guests to his pet crocodile. While lacking Chain Saw's raw documentary-style terror, Eaten Alive cranks up the psychedelic lighting and surreal atmosphere that would later influence Italian horror masters like Lucio Fulci's The Beyond (1981).

sections.content: The film's garish neon lighting and claustrophobic sets create a fever-dream quality that sets it apart from other 1970s exploitation films. Hooper uses the same suffocating Texas atmosphere as Chain Saw but adds layers of psychosexual tension and Grand Guignol gore. The influence is clear in later Southern-fried horror like Eaten (2007) and Crawl (2019), though none match the raw, unhinged energy of Brand's performance as the mentally unstable Judd.

While often overlooked in Hooper's filmography between The Texas Chain Saw Massacre (1974) and Salem's Lot (1979), Eaten Alive showcases his talent for creating oppressive atmosphere and managing sustained tension. The film's mix of psychological horror and creature feature elements would later influence hybrid films like Rogue (2007) and Black Water (2007). SUBHEAD: Impact on Aquatic Horror

sections.content: Eaten Alive helped establish tropes that would become staples of the aquatic horror subgenre - the isolated location, the unhinged authority figure, and the blending of human and animal threats. These elements appear in everything from Lake Placid (1999) to Crawl (2019). The film's influence extends beyond simple creature features into psychological horror territory, seen in films like Black Water: Abyss (2020).
